html:
The 1991 Iraqi uprisings were revolts in March 1991 by Shia Arabs in southern Iraq and Kurds in the north against Saddam Hussein, right after Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War.

The south rose first, in Basra, Najaf and Karbala, and the Kurdish north followed within days. President George H. W. Bush had urged Iraqis to take matters into their own hands. The rebels expected help. The coalition did not give it, partly out of fear that Iraq would break up and that Iran would gain.

Saddam's Republican Guard kept its best units and its helicopters. It crushed the south in a few weeks, with heavy killing. Estimates of the dead run from tens of thousands to well over 100,000. In the north about a million Kurds fled toward the Turkish and Iranian borders.

The scenes of refugees in the mountains led the coalition to set up a safe haven in northern Iraq, and no-fly zones over the north and, from 1992, over the south. The southern marshes were later drained. The north became the base of today's Kurdistan Region. Shia bitterness at the betrayal lasted until 2003.
sum: The 1991 Iraqi uprisings were revolts in March 1991 by Shia Arabs in southern Iraq and Kurds in the north against Saddam Hussein, right after Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War.
